implementation_notes: Python's stripe primitive is threading.Lock (a thin wrapper over the platform mutex); the idiom is a list of N locks plus a mapping such as a stable hash modulo N, or a defaultdict of per-key RLock when keys are few. Under the GIL only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time, so striping pays off mainly when the critical section releases the GIL (I/O, C extensions such as sqlite3 or numpy) or on free-threaded builds (PEP 703, Python 3.13+ with --disable-gil), where the locks become the real concurrency primitive. For a plain keyed store, prefer a dict guarded by one lock or an existing concurrent container over hand-rolled striping.
code_sketch:
STRIPES = [threading.Lock() for _ in range(64)]

def put(key, value):
    with STRIPES[stable_hash(key) % len(STRIPES)]:
        state[key] = value

# multi-key: for i in sorted({stable_hash(k) % len(STRIPES) for k in keys}): ...
pitfalls: str hash() is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED) and user hashes can change with mutable state; use hashlib.blake2b or zlib.crc32 when stripe placement must be reproducible or keys are mutable.

The GIL makes some code accidentally correct: moving from one lock to stripes (or to a free-threaded build) can expose races in sequences that relied on bytecode atomicity, so audit the critical section rather than assume the lock was redundant.
threading.Lock is not reentrant; nested acquisition of the same stripe needs RLock, and multi-stripe acquisition must use a fixed sorted order to avoid deadlock.
